idiom_name: function type (T) -> Unit with a lambda; suspend functions for asynchronous completion
implementation_notes: Kotlin makes the callback a language-level value type: a parameter of type (Result) -> Unit accepts a lambda or a function reference, and a named callback type only needs the fun interface modifier (or a Java interface) for SAM conversion. The interface-implementation structure remains for multi-method listeners, and for asynchronous work the idiomatic replacement is a suspend function or a callback-to-Flow bridge (callbackFlow, suspendCancellableCoroutine), because structured concurrency and cancellation replace the manual lifetime bookkeeping of a stored callback. Pass the lambda inline (trailing lambda syntax) so the compiler can keep it allocation-free, and mark callback-taking higher-order functions inline when the callback runs synchronously.
pitfalls: A lambda captures variables into a shared box; a callback that runs on another thread and mutates the same variable needs explicit synchronization.
A Kotlin-declared interface is SAM-converted from a lambda only with fun interface (Java interfaces convert freely), which changes the public shape of the API.

Coroutine cancellation does not cancel callbacks already handed to third-party code, so a cancelled job can still receive a completion unless the source honours the cancellation handle (this is what callbackFlow's awaitClose exists for).
A return inside a lambda passed to an inline function is a non-local return from the enclosing function, which hides control flow from the reader.
